summary: Foula Airfield (FOA) is a small airfield serving Foula, one of the most remote permanently inhabited islands in the United Kingdom, located in the Shetland archipelago off the north coast of Scotland. The island, home to a tiny community of around 30 residents, relies on this airstrip alongside occasional ferry service for connections to the Shetland mainland. The remote location, dramatic cliffs, and surrounding North Atlantic waters make Foula a distinctive destination for visitors seeking an isolated and unspoiled landscape.
faqs:
Q: How do you get to Foula Airfield?
A: Flights to Foula typically operate from Tingwall or Sumburgh in Shetland on small aircraft, with services subject to weather conditions due to the island's exposed position in the North Atlantic.

Q: Are there scheduled flights to Foula?
A: Yes, a small scheduled air service connects Foula with Shetland's mainland, though frequency is limited and flights can be cancelled due to adverse weather.

Q: What facilities are available at Foula Airfield?
A: Foula Airfield is a minimal grass-strip facility with no terminal building or commercial amenities; passengers should arrange transport and accommodation on the island in advance.

Q: Can you visit Foula as a tourist?
A: Yes, Foula welcomes visitors interested in birdwatching, hiking, and experiencing one of Britain's most isolated inhabited islands, though arrangements must be made in advance.
transport_tips: Foula Airfield has no public transport links, so visitors must pre-arrange accommodation and any onward travel on the island with their hosts. Flights are weather-dependent and may be cancelled with little notice, so building flexibility into your travel plans is essential. The nearest connecting airports are Tingwall and Sumburgh in Shetland, which have links to Aberdeen and Edinburgh.
local_tip: Bring layered, windproof clothing regardless of season—Foula's cliffs and open terrain are famously exposed to Atlantic weather, and conditions can change rapidly even on seemingly calm days.
